# Results — Study 899 (Cash + Call "90/10")

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — Bill **Gross's
"90/10"** (and Bodie's "T-bills + calls"): keep ~90% in T-bills so capital is roughly preserved and
spend ~10% on **convex upside** via call options. Does the asymmetric "protect capital, rent upside"
profile beat plain buy-and-hold on **risk-adjusted** terms across 2008 / 2020 / 2022? Because listed
single-name / index option history is not freely available, the ~10% sleeve is a **documented
proxy** — a rolling **1-year at-the-money SPY call marked daily with Black–Scholes** (strike = spot
at each annual roll, priced off SPY's trailing realized vol and the ^IRX bill rate; the 10% budget
buys as much notional as the fair price affords, capped at ~100% of NAV). Offline & deterministic
once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. Data as-of 2026-06-30 (the
last complete calendar month; the partial current month is dropped). Fingerprint `b954e845292f`
(SPY total-return, BIL total-return, ^IRX rate).*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily closes: **SPY** (`auto_adjust=True`, total return — the underlying path), **BIL** (1–3m T-bills, the cash leg *and* the excess-of-cash denominator), **^IRX** (13-week T-bill rate, the Black–Scholes risk-free input), **2007-05-31 → 2026-06-30**, 4,799 return rows |
| 90/10 rule | each **annual roll** buys a fresh **1-yr ATM SPY call** (`K = spot`) to insure up to **100%** of NAV in upside; if the Black–Scholes premium ≤ **10%** of NAV it takes full cover and banks the change in BIL, else it spends the whole 10% budget on partial cover; the call is **marked daily** (spot / vol / rate / time-to-expiry), the rest sits in BIL; state read at the previous close (zero look-ahead) |
| Proxy caveats (Signal-axis) | **Black–Scholes model risk** (a real listed call trades at *implied* vol, not realized — see the premium sweep); the call-holder **forgoes the SPY dividend** (~1.8%/yr), a small optimistic tilt; a single strike/tenor grid |
| Benchmarks | **buy-and-hold** 100% SPY (the upside the premium is paid out of) and a **matched static mix** — a constant-mix book rebalanced daily to 90/10's realized average **delta-weight** (isolates the *convexity* question) |
| Fair race | all three books measured **excess-of-cash** (minus BIL); a constant fraction of SPY has the *same* excess-Sharpe as SPY, so the static and buy-and-hold Sharpes coincide and the honest read on the option's non-linearity is the **convexity spanning alpha** (90/10 on static, HAC *t* on the intercept) |
| Statistics | leverage/level-clean spanning alpha; a circular block-bootstrap CI on the excess-**Sharpe difference**; a HAC *t* on the daily excess-return difference; a two-era cut; a **premium (vol-risk-premium) sweep** and a cost sweep; the up/down capture asymmetry; a 30-seed synthetic control |

**Short history — named on the Signal axis.** BIL (the cash leg) lists **2007-05-30**, bounding the
joint window to ~19 years — one GFC-anchored cycle, not a law. It is a *favourable* draw for a
capital-protection rule, though: it contains **2008, 2020 and 2022**, exactly the crashes the floor
is built for.

## The race — 90/10 vs buy-and-hold vs matched static mix (excess-of-cash, gross, BS-fair premium)

| book | excess Sharpe | Sortino | CAGR | vol | max drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **90/10** (1-yr ATM call, ≤10% budget) | **0.492** | 0.497 | 6.13% | 10.42% | **−19.8%** |
| buy-and-hold SPY | **0.543** | 0.513 | 10.70% | 19.78% | **−55.2%** |
| matched static mix (avg Δ-w = 0.68) | 0.543 | 0.513 | 8.09% | 13.44% | −40.2% |

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| excess-Sharpe vs buy-and-hold | **−0.051** |
| excess-Sharpe vs matched static | −0.051 *(identical — the constant-fraction identity)* |
| convexity spanning alpha (90/10 on static) | **+0.46%/yr**, HAC ***t* = +0.33** (β = 0.638) |
| raw excess-diff HAC *t* | −1.37 |
| up-capture / down-capture (asymmetry) | 0.564 / 0.568 (**−0.003**) |
| avg Δ-weight / roll turnover | 0.68 / **0.18×/yr** |

Capital protection is **real and large**: max drawdown **−19.8%** versus buy-and-hold's **−55.2%**,
at roughly **half the volatility** (10.4% vs 19.8%). But the headline "beats buy-and-hold on
risk-adjusted terms" claim is **not** met — 90/10's excess-of-cash **Sharpe (0.492) essentially
ties** buy-and-hold's (0.543): the gap is **−0.05**, and the option's **convexity adds nothing**
measurable over the same average linear exposure (spanning α **+0.46%/yr, *t* = +0.33**; up- and
down-capture are symmetric to 0.003). Read plainly: 90/10 is a **de-risked equity position** whose
Sharpe is pinned to SPY's by the constant-fraction identity — the call wrapper reshapes the *tail*,
not the risk-adjusted *return*. And this is measured at the **Black–Scholes-fair** premium, which
*understates* real option costs (see below).

## Bootstrap — circular block CI on the excess-Sharpe difference, 90/10 − buy-and-hold (2,000 resamples)

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| Sharpe gain | **−0.051** |
| 95% CI | **[−0.334, +0.210]** |
| P(90/10 wins) | **33.8%** |

**The CI straddles zero.** 90/10's Sharpe is statistically **indistinguishable** from buy-and-hold's
— neither a robust edge nor a clear shortfall. There is no significant risk-adjusted *return* signal
to bank; what is real is the drawdown reduction.

## Crash years — does capital protection bite? (calendar-year total return & worst intra-year drawdown)

| year | buy-and-hold | 90/10 |
|---|--:|--:|
| **2008** | −36.8% (DD −47.1%) | **−8.1% (DD −10.2%)** |
| **2020** | +18.3% (DD −33.7%) | **−1.1% (DD −15.7%)** |
| **2022** | −18.2% (DD −24.5%) | **−17.1% (DD −19.6%)** |

**2008 is the profile's finest hour** — a −47% peak-to-trough cut to −10% (the calls expired
worthless, the bills carried the book). **2020** shows the honest cost of *renting* rather than
*owning* the upside: 90/10 protected the crash but its capped-notional, expensive-vol calls captured
little of the V-shaped snap-back, turning buy-and-hold's **+18.3%** into **−1.1%**. And **2022's slow
grind** was barely helped (−17.1% vs −18.2%): a drawn-out bear that never spikes vol gives the call
sleeve nothing to protect against while the premium bleeds. Capital protection is genuine for the
*crash* it is shaped for — and you pay for it in every quiet year.

## Robustness — two eras (split 2016-01-01)

| era | n | 90/10 Sharpe | BH Sharpe | vs-BH | convexity α *t* | maxDD 90/10 vs BH |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2007-05 → 2015-12 | 2,163 | +0.453 | +0.335 | **+0.119** | +0.94 | −19.8% vs −55.2% |
| 2016-01 → 2026-06 | 2,635 | +0.999 | +0.767 | **+0.232** | +1.68 | −11.1% vs −33.7% |

Each half is *individually* a shade **favourable** to 90/10 (vs-BH +0.12 and +0.23) — yet the pooled
Sharpe gap is slightly negative (−0.05), the usual Sharpe-is-not-additive artefact of mixing a
high-vol GFC regime with a calmer one. Crucially, **neither era's convexity alpha clears
significance** (*t* = +0.94, +1.68 < 2). So the sign is not stable enough, nor the alpha strong
enough, to call a real risk-adjusted edge — while the drawdown protection is large in *both* eras.

## Premium sweep — the tradability crux (real calls cost more than BS-fair: the variance risk premium)

The Black–Scholes price above uses *realized* vol; a real listed 1-yr ATM call trades at *implied*
vol, which sits **above** realized (the variance risk premium — IV/RV ≈ 1.1–1.4 on the S&P). The
`prem_mult` knob scales the option cost to that reality:

| option cost (×BS-fair) | 90/10 Sharpe | vs-BH | avg Δ-w | maxDD |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.80 (unrealistically cheap) | +0.629 | **+0.087** | 0.70 | −18.3% |
| **1.00 (BS-fair, realized vol)** | **0.492** | **−0.051** | 0.68 | −19.8% |
| 1.25 (mild vol-risk premium) | +0.335 | **−0.208** | 0.66 | −21.1% |
| 1.50 (typical listed markup) | +0.193 | **−0.350** | 0.63 | −21.6% |
| 2.00 (stressed / crisis IV) | −0.039 | −0.582 | 0.56 | −26.7% |

**The near-tie exists only at the fictional BS-fair price.** Charge the option what it actually costs
— a **1.25–1.5×** IV/RV markup — and 90/10's excess Sharpe drops to **−0.21…−0.35**, decisively below
buy-and-hold. The parity was a mirage of ignoring the variance risk premium (and, on top, the
forgone dividend). Renting upside is a *net-negative-carry* trade priced to leave the buyer behind.

## Costed — one-way bps on the roll notional (annual roll ⇒ negligible turnover)

| one-way cost | 90/10 Sharpe | BH Sharpe | vs-BH | maxDD (90/10) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bp | 0.492 | 0.543 | −0.051 | −19.8% |
| 10 bp | 0.492 | 0.543 | −0.051 | −19.8% |
| 50 bp | 0.492 | 0.543 | −0.051 | −19.8% |

Turnover is a trivial **0.18×/yr** (one option roll a year), so *trading* costs are a rounding error
— this is **not a friction story**. The tradability problem is entirely in the **premium** the option
demands (the table above), not the commission to trade it.

## Synthetic control — the machinery is unbiased

Deterministic seeded worlds (no network). The mechanical claim is capital protection, so the
positive control is a **bear** tape where the drawdown floor must visibly hold; the null is a
**calm** steady bull where nothing draws down and the premium simply bleeds; an **up-jump** tape
checks the convex sleeve rides positive skew.

| world | reads |
|---|--:|
| **bear** (drift < 0), **30 seeds** | drawdown protection mean **+0.369** (min +0.043), avg Δ-weight **de-risks to 0.41** ⇒ capital protected mechanically |
| **calm** steady bull, **30 seeds** | avg Δ-weight **0.79** (> bear's — the rule de-risks as vol rises); 90/10 **gives up upside** (lower CAGR than buy-and-hold) in **30/30** |
| **up-jump** positive-skew, 10 seeds | still protects the drawdown (mean **+0.042**) while the jumps lift the upside — the convex floor holds |

The engine protects capital in a fall, de-risks as vol rises, and never levers past full capital in
calm markets — so the real-tape reads are genuine properties of the SPY tape, not a broken engine.
*(A faithful-engine / power check only — never cited in support of the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The **capital-protection claim is real and mechanical**: max drawdown
  **−19.8% vs buy-and-hold's −55.2%** at half the vol, 2008 cut from −47% to −10%, and a 30-seed
  synthetic control confirms the engine floors the drawdown and de-risks into vol. But the claim the
  desk grades — *"beats buy-and-hold on risk-adjusted terms"* — is **not** met: even at the
  optimistic Black–Scholes-fair premium the excess-of-cash **Sharpe (0.492) ties** buy-and-hold's
  (0.543), the difference **−0.051** with a **bootstrap 95% CI [−0.334, +0.210]** through zero
  (P(win) 34%), the option's **convexity adds no measurable alpha** (spanning α +0.46%/yr, *t* =
  +0.33; symmetric up/down capture), and the two eras, while individually a touch favourable, do not
  clear significance (α *t* < 2). A single GFC-anchored ~19-year window, with a BS-marked proxy that
  *flatters* the strategy (realized-vol pricing, no dividend drag). **Real risk reduction, no robust
  risk-adjusted edge.**
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The Sharpe parity is a **mirage of the fair-premium assumption**. A real
  listed 1-yr ATM call carries the **variance risk premium** (IV > RV): price the option at a
  realistic **1.25–1.5× markup** and 90/10's excess Sharpe falls to **−0.21…−0.35**, decisively below
  buy-and-hold — and the call-holder also **forgoes the ~1.8%/yr dividend**. This is *not* a friction
  story (annual roll ⇒ 0.18×/yr turnover, costs are a rounding error); it is that renting upside is
  priced to leave the buyer behind. Even in the best case it only **matches** buy-and-hold's Sharpe
  while giving up **~4.6%/yr of CAGR** — a payoff reshaping (own the tail, not the return), not a
  paycheck. You run 90/10 to sleep at night, not to get paid.
